result.text:
An AI agent can now prove it was allowed to act.
It still can’t prove what it actually did.
Authorization is a snapshot.
Behavior is the film.

A signed permission at 9:00 tells you what the agent was allowed to do.
It says nothing about the sequence of decisions it made at 9:05, which data it trusted, where a human intervened, or what the real-world outcome was.
As agents move from answering questions to operating systems, modifying production databases, and controlling physical processes, this gap becomes the critical failure point. When something goes wrong, most teams still can’t reconstruct a clean, independently verifiable chain of events. They have logs. They don’t have evidence.

This is the same problem aviation solved decades ago. A pilot’s license doesn’t explain a crash. The flight recorder does. It captures what happened, in order, with enough integrity that outsiders can check it.
AI agents are entering the same phase. The more autonomous they become, the more they need a behavioral record that can be audited after the fact, not just an execution log that the system itself controls.

The companies that close this loop will have something models alone can’t deliver: a continuous, verifiable feedback signal from real actions and real outcomes. Everyone else will keep generating more output while remaining unable to prove what actually occurred.

Generation is getting cheaper.
Proof of what happened is still scarce.

That’s the layer Proof of Human Action (PoHA) is built to provide: an immutable record that links authorization, the actions that were actually taken, and the outcomes that followed. Not another claim. Not another log. Evidence that can be checked independently.

Can your agents show their work?
#Actum #POHA #IndustrialDePIN #VerifiedBehavior
